about: Constraints checked after binding: declared choices, required flags, variadic bounds, and the relationships between flags. These do not affect which token binds where, only whether the result is accepted.

vectors.doc: A value among the declared choices is accepted.
A value outside the declared choices is rejected.
Choices match exactly. Case-insensitive matching would have to be declared, not assumed.
Positionals carry choices too.
Each value a variadic collects is checked, not only the first. A list that is valid up to its last element is not a valid list.
The same for a repeatable flag: every occurrence carries a value, and every value is checked.
Choices constrain the value, not the command line, so a value arriving from `env` is checked like any other. Otherwise the environment would be a way around the declaration.
A required flag that is given parses normally.
A required flag that is absent is an error.
`required_unless` is satisfied when the named alternative is present.
With neither flag present, the requirement stands.
Two flags that override each other leave only the last one given.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" overrides="--stdin"
flag "--stdin" overrides="--file"

vectors.doc: The command line said `--stdin` came last, so `--file` lost. A flag that lost an override is not merely unset: filling it from the environment afterwards would leave both standing and undo the last-one-wins.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" env="EX_FILE" overrides="--stdin"
flag "--stdin"

vectors.doc: `--trace` came last, so `--log-level` lost and holds nothing by the end. That settles which of the two is in effect; it does not make `v` one of the choices. Only a later occurrence of `--log-level` itself can replace the word it was given — a different flag winning the pair is not a correction of what was typed.
Two flags declared to conflict cannot be given together. Unlike `overrides`, where the last one wins, a conflict is a mistake to report rather than an order to resolve.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" conflicts="--stdin"
flag "--stdin"
flag "--url <url>"

vectors.doc: The conflict is declared on `--file` only, and still applies when `--stdin` comes first: the relationship is between the two flags, not between a flag and the tokens after it.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" conflicts="--stdin"
flag "--stdin"
flag "--url <url>"

vectors.doc: A declared conflict costs nothing when only one side is given.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" conflicts="--stdin"
flag "--stdin"
flag "--url <url>"

vectors.doc: Only the named flag conflicts; an unnamed one alongside it is fine.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" conflicts="--stdin"
flag "--stdin"
flag "--url <url>"

vectors.doc: A value from the environment counts as given: `--file` conflicts with `--stdin` even though only `--stdin` was typed. clap, argparse and usage all treat an environment variable as a value source rather than as a weaker kind of default.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" env="EX_FILE" conflicts="--stdin"
flag "--stdin" env="EX_STDIN"

vectors.doc: Neither side was typed and the conflict still holds, which is what makes the rule uniform: the check asks whether a flag has a value, not how it got one.
vectors.spec:
name "ex"
bin "ex"
flag "--file <file>" env="EX_FILE" conflicts="--stdin"
flag "--stdin" env="EX_STDIN"

vectors.doc: `var_min` is enforced for a repeatable flag, not only for positionals.
`var_max` is likewise enforced for a repeatable flag.
A value-conditional requirement is enforced when the declaring flag explicitly has the named value.
A different value does not activate the conditional requirement.
The conditional requirement disappears once the flag it names has a value.
An environment value is explicit and activates a matching conditional requirement, as it does in clap.
A default does not activate a value-conditional requirement because nobody supplied it.
